Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How are you doing today? I hope you are doing great out there.
Answer: Great! I am in Playa del Carmen, Mexico. I had an amazing dinner with a beautiful Italian woman who was gracious enough to laugh at my jokes. I was also happy that she understand my Spanish, since she only spoke Spanish and Italian. Even though I’m pretty much fluent in Spanish, my pronunciation can be rough and not always understood. Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What is the worst country you have ever visited?
Answer: Besides an obvious country like Kuwait, the worst country I have visited was Argentina. The people were cold, unfriendly. I was anxious my entire time there. I spoke Spanish as best as I could with anyone that would listen. From the moment I landed at the airport in Mendoza I was detained by the police, I was interrogated and asked where I was coming from and where I was going (I believe they thought I was Venezuelan.) When they realized I was from the US, they let me go. I think it’s regrettable I had such a poor experience in Argentina, because Buenos Aires and Mendoza are very beautiful cities. I would still go to Argentina again probably, but now I am more prepared to receive an unfriendly welcome. I am hesitant to blame the poor time I had in Argentina on my dark skin, but I believe it probably played a part. Oh well. (Downtown Buenos Aires. Photo by author.)

Question: If you have a chance to have a drink with any historical figure, who would you choose and what would you talk about?
Answer: I had to think about this, my first instinct was to say Churchill or Eisenhower. However, when I thought about it, I’d have to go with Marcus Aurelius. He’d probably prefer to have wine, but if he was open to it, I’d share a bottle of a single malt scotch with him. I’d ask him about being a good leader, his favorite foods, and why his son, Commodus, is such a dick.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Why should you respect a veteran?
Answer: I think, collectively, as a nation it is good to both respect and honor our veterans that make countless sacrifices and give years of their life to the military — often times — the best ones. This is doubly so when we talk about veterans who have fought in combat, have been wounded or captured, and other heroic deeds. They represent some of the finest human beings I have ever had the pleasure to be around. The ultimate respect a nation can give veterans is to ensure they have the support they need when they return home, and that they have the tools to build a stable life, if at all possible. (John McCain, after returning from Vietnam where he’d been a prisoner of war in the infamous “Hanoi Hilton” prison. To me, John McCain is an example of veteran who was undoubtedly a hero for his nation, but your feelings may differ, especially based on your political outlook. Photo Credit: AP.) I am opposed to, however, the idea that each person, individually, needs to go out of their way to show respect to most veterans. My libertarian leanings also require that I mention it becomes a little creepy when patriotism bleeds into the area of unconditional hero worship. Most veterans are fallible human beings, with a wide diversity of political beliefs, backgrounds, mores, and even sexual preferences. There’s a non-zero chance that if you meet some of the people you call your hero, you may not even like them. Lastly, most of us didn’t see much combat. We probably had jobs that were tough compared to the average person, but so does a lumberjack.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What was the best thing about being a child of your generation?
Answer: We were the last generation without social media during our childhood. Facebook was brand new just as I hit college. Although bullying was a problem in the 1990’s, it was mostly limited to school hours or day camp (during the summers). There was no fear of missing out. The only way to know what your friends were doing during summers and weekends was to be there with them or have them tell you about it when they saw you again. Even taking a lot of pictures was rare since film was still expensive and photography still an art. (Images like this automatically induce anxiety in 90’s kids. Source: Washington Post.) Entertainment for kids sucked in comparison to today. Sure, I think our video games were pretty fun, but they didn’t offer realistic and immersive worlds like they do today. Even if you could play for more than 3–4 hours at a time, eventually, the sun and sky would call and seem more appealing. Video games were best left for rainy days. More imaginative entertainment would take place during summers. You’d also occasionally read books. Many of the things that are health risks today weren’t considered during my childhood. On one hand, it meant that child car seats weren’t a thing and no one cared about secondhand smoke. On the other, it meant that we ate lots of candy, drank lots of soda, had fried foods, and occasionally, were given alcohol by adults. It never occurred to either us or our parents that our generation would end up fat and unhealthy. This ignorance was bliss.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Younger guys, do you like older women?
Answer: Yes, almost exclusively. I get made fun of sometimes by my buddies, but I have never enjoyed dating women my own age. There is something more enigmatic, intoxicating about older women. Furthermore, they are almost always straight to the point. If an older woman doesn’t like you, she tells you. She doesn’t have time to waste. There is also something incredibly beautiful about the body of a woman who has lived her life. Scars, gray hairs, wrinkles. The signs of a life well-lived. An older woman can tell you where you’re headed, because she has already been there. (Jennifer Coolidge. To people my age she will always be known as Stifler’s mom. A generation of young men lusted after her. Photo credit: Buzz Feed.)
